analysis: The closest option has a progression from sociology to modern and contemporary social theory, with ethnographic and other qualitative techniques, empirical design and critical use of historical evidence. Histories of gender, empire and Indigenous peoples give comparative cases. Rights, global political institutions and conflict address power and development. The redesign replaces generic stylistics, rhetoric and literary interpretation with survey methods, environmental justice and Indigenous history. UCR does not have a dedicated anthropology sequence or a separately required month of ethnographic fieldwork.

The environmental option gives priority to climate, resource use, water management, human and nonhuman relationships, and community responses. Ecology supports interpretation of environmental pressures. Governance and justice apply social research to institutional responses. The partner project supplies applied research experience and is taken in its planned first semester. Coastal adaptation and life-cycle analysis replace sustainability gateways and geochemistry to strengthen the connection to communities and resource choices.

The media option begins with film analysis and media history, then studies representation in television, digital media, African art, museums and documentary. Social theory and qualitative research support its investigation of culture and power. AI ethics and data work are complementary to digital media study. Comparative histories and Indigenous perspectives contextualise the subjects of visual work. The composition does not claim specialist digital ethnography or a visual anthropology degree.

The alternatives differ by 67.5, 60 and 82.5 EC each way. The closest option has substantial global politics and inequality coverage. The environmental option gives depth in ecology, adaptation and governance, and the visual option gives depth in visual representation and production. Body, health and applied anthropology remain a coherent unselected direction at the three-option limit.
constructionStop: Three academically viable and distinct compositions meet the maximum.

alignment.rationale: Both use historical comparison to study political power and global connections. UCR concentrates on empires, while UvA links local practices with development and globalisation.
Both introduce social theory and the study of identity and social relations. UvA develops these questions through anthropology.
Both teach qualitative research design, interviews, observation and interpretation. UvA applies these methods in a disciplinary anthropology sequence.
Both examine changes in social theory, including feminist and postcolonial approaches. UvA focuses on the history of anthropology.
Both use contemporary social theory to examine power, inequality and collective responses. UvA works through anthropological monographs and current global issues.
UvA develops critical reading and writing through ethnographic monographs. UCR develops related reading and writing across several courses.
UCR introduces questions about knowledge and belief. UvA studies how scientific knowledge is produced and contested in society.
UvA brings together professional anthropology, reflection and a practical exercise.
UvA requires a month of ethnographic fieldwork and combines group inquiry with individual writing. UCR teaches field methods within Qualitative Research Methodology.
Students complete two 6 EC courses in the discipline.
Students complete one 6 EC regional anthropology course.
Students choose one 12 EC anthropology theme course per semester. Documentary is relevant to visual anthropology among the available choices.
Each selected theme has a linked 3 EC presentation.
This is 6 EC of open elective space.
UvA requires professional planning and career preparation at the end of the degree.
UvA requires students to develop a profile for professional work in anthropology.
This is 24 EC of open elective space.
